extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, literary students, and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and critical guidance for novelists on character, point of view, and plot — how to construct flat vs round characters, choose and manage narrative viewpoint, and design plots that balance causality, mystery, and economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat characters (also called ‘humorous’, types, or caricatures) are constructed round a single idea or quality and can be expressed in one sentence (e.g., “I never will desert Mr. Micawber”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages and uses: easily recognized by the reader’s emotional eye, never need reintroducing, do not require development, provide their own atmosphere, and are easily remembered—useful for convenience, permanence, and comic effect (examples: Mrs. Micawber, Caleb Balderstone, Proust’s Princess of Parma or Legrandin). Disadvantages: not as large an achievement as round characters; a serious or tragic flat character tends to bore; formulaic repetition can deaden interest. Flat characters work best when combined with other kinds to supply contrast and to be animated by the author’s force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Round characters cannot be summed up in a single phrase; they have complexity, private desires and aches, and the capacity to change and surprise (examples: principal characters in War and Peace, Dostoevsky characters, Madame Bovary, Becky Sharp).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test: a round character is ‘capable of surprising in a convincing way.’ If it never surprises, it is flat; if it surprises without convincing, it is a flat pretending to be round. Round characters have a ‘secret life’ and can expand when given space; they are fit to perform tragically and to move readers beyond humour and appropriateness. Make round characters 'ready for an extended life'—organized to function all round rather than tethered to a single formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine flat and round characters
rubrics_metrics.description: A complex novel often requires both flat and round people; the collisions between types and complex characters can better parallel life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use flat characters for economy, recognizability, and to provide immediate atmosphere; use round characters for depth and development. Examples: Dickens largely uses types yet achieves depth through vitality; Wells and Dickens can 'galvanize' flat parts by transmitting force from the living parts of the work. Balance both kinds to harmonize the human range in the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist may describe characters from outside (impartial/partial onlooker), assume omniscience, place the narrative in the position of one character (limited/first-person), or adopt intermediate attitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be conscious of the relation between narrator and story. Shifting viewpoint can succeed if the writer has the power to 'bounce the reader into accepting what he says' (examples: Dickens’ shifting POVs in Bleak House; Tolstoy’s intermittent knowledge in War and Peace). Excessively obvious or self-conscious shifts (author over-explaining jolts) can cool the emotional effect and make the work merely 'interesting' rather than vital (example: Gide).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid authorial confidences about individual characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not take the reader into the novelist’s confidence about the individual people in the book (e.g., asides like 'she always was my favourite').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such confidences generally lead to a drop in emotional temperature, intellectual laxity, facetiousness, and 'bar-parlour chattiness' that destroys illusion and nobility. It is safer to generalize about the universe or conditions of life than to intimate private authorial asides about characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict the secret life and subconscious convincingly
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel’s special privilege is access to self-communings and the subconscious; the novelist can talk about characters as well as through them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interiority and subconscious material freely, but ensure shifts into minds and back again are convincing to the reader. Do not be overly concerned with 'how the writer knew' if the presentation is convincing; legalistic objections to shifting viewpoint are irrelevant if the reader accepts the truth of the depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as causality (distinct from story)
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot is a narrative of events with emphasis on causality (e.g., 'The king died, and then the queen died of grief'); a story is mere time-sequence ('the king died and then the queen died').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plot suspends time-sequence to ask 'why' and often incorporates mystery. It requires the reader’s intelligence and memory to perceive cross-correspondences and causal chains. A successful plot arranges events so that the eventual revelation feels aesthetically compact; it is not simply a chain of 'and then' episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for intelligence and memory, not mere curiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Curiosity alone drives story (the 'and then' reader); plot demands intelligence and memory so the reader can hold facts in relation and detect mysteries and clues over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide cross-correspondences and clues that repay an intelligent, remembering reader; expect the reader to brood and rearrange facts as the book unfolds. Avoid writing solely to titillate curiosity; cultivate puzzles and suspensions that later cohere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and organic unity in plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Every action or word in a plot ought to count; the plot should be economical, spare, organic, and free from dead-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leave no loose ends and avoid misleading the reader gratuitously. Even when complex or mysterious, the plot should feel necessary and economized so that the final sense is 'aesthetically compact'—beauty may emerge as an accidental result of good plotting but should not be the explicit aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters must contribute to the plot; avoid excessive brooding
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters in a novel are often enormous and intractable, but they must still 'contribute' to the plot; they must not brood so long that higher interests (the plot) are jeopardized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While novels allow interior wandering, the author must ensure characters do not waste time in self-absorption to the detriment of causality. The plot-maker expects contributions; when characters fail to act, narrative energy and unity suffer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrivances that spring from character and cause surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrivances (incidents or devices) are acceptable when they arise from characters and then react upon them, producing surprise and transformation (illustrated by Meredith’s 'contrivances').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-designed contrivances should feel organic—unexpected yet natural—provoking shocks that change personages and advance the book. The proper shock produces a response of 'Oh, that’s all right' and signals a healthy relation between character and plot.
